Imagine you’re running a fashion brand with 1,000 products. Or perhaps you’re a freelance creative working on a product campaign, or part of a brand’s marketing team responsible for producing hundreds of images for an upcoming collection. New collections are arriving. Existing products need updated photographs. Marketing teams are preparing seasonal campaigns, the ecommerce team needs fresh visuals, and social media requires a constant stream of content. Now multiply that work across hundreds of products, different colors, multiple formats, and different campaign concepts. The challenge isn’t knowing what you want your brand to look like. It’s producing everything needed to bring that vision to life. And here’s the problem: the more products a brand manages, the more complicated creative production becomes. AI image generation has made creating individual images remarkably accessible. But generating an impressive image and managing visual production for an entire product catalog are two very different challenges. Creating images one by one, repeating prompts, adjusting settings, maintaining consistency, and organizing outputs can quickly become another time-consuming process. At AgentDocks , we believe the solution isn’t simply giving brands access to more AI models. It’s giving them a way to automate the creative work those models perform. One Product Image. An Entire Creative Direction. Let’s look at an actual workflow we created in AgentDocks. For this example, we built a ready-to-use handbag photography workflow designed to transform a simple product image into multiple premium fashion visuals. The concept is straightforward. A brand uploads a photograph of its handbag, and the workflow handles a series of predefined creative tasks. Instead of manually generating every image, the workflow connects several generation steps, each with its own purpose. One creates a clean editorial photograph featuring the handbag. Another places it on a fashion model. Others explore different compositions, close-ups, product arrangements, and campaign styling. The creative direction, prompts, AI models, and connections are already prepared. The user doesn’t need to reconstruct the setup for every output. They provide the product image and run the workflow. One input. Multiple creative results. One connected production process. Press enter or click to view image in full size Caption: A handbag photography workflow built in AgentDocks. Product images are connected to multiple AI generation steps, producing a collection of fashion and editorial visuals from a reusable creative setup. What makes this particularly useful isn’t just the images themselves. It’s the fact that the entire process can be reused. Imagine a handbag brand releasing 20 new designs. Instead of rebuilding the same campaign setup for every bag, the team can return to the workflow, change the product inputs, and generate new variations following the established creative direction. And when the collection expands again, the production system is already there. That’s the real shift we’re interested in: moving from creating individual assets to creating systems that produce them. When Your Catalog Grows, Your Workload Shouldn’t Grow at the Same Rate For brands managing hundreds or thousands of SKUs, producing content isn’t a one-time activity. Every new collection introduces more work. Product launches require ecommerce photography, social content, promotional campaigns, and visuals adapted to different channels. Traditionally, scaling content often means coordinating additional resources, extending production schedules, or simplifying the creative work. AI automation introduces another approach. With Batch Run , AgentDocks allows teams to apply the same creative workflow to a collection of product images automatically. Instead of manually uploading and generating each product separately, teams can process up to 50 images per batch, then reuse the workflow for additional collections. For a catalog of 1,000 products, that means working through successive batches without having to recreate the production process for every SKU. The same idea applies to other industries. A skincare company might need consistent product photography across serums, moisturizers, and cleansers. A fashion retailer might need on-model images for dozens of clothing variations. An accessories brand might need editorial visuals for every product in a new seasonal collection. In each case, the creative direction can be developed once, tested, refined, and reused across the product range.
